Subject: Please read this one — the blue pills, and what to do if someone goes down

I'm Becky, I'm local and I work in ICU. I've just come off nights so I'll keep it as short as I can, but I didn't want to leave this till I'd slept.

First off, I'm not going to say anything about anyone I've looked after. Not who, not how old, nothing. That's not mine to share and it wouldn't help anyway. What I will do is tell you what I'd want every parent and every teenager on this group to know, because the notice from the police is sat up there and people are scrolling past it.

The blue tablets going round are being sold as diazepam or "Xanax". Some of them have nitazenes in them. Nitazenes are synthetic opioids and they can be far stronger than heroin. You can't tell by looking at them. You can't tell by who sold them to you, or how well you know them.

What to watch for: extreme drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, slow or noisy breathing, blue lips. If you see any of that, it's an emergency, not someone having a heavy one.

The police have said it themselves — their priority is preserving life. Preserving life. Not prosecuting the mate who rang. So if someone goes down, you ring 999 straight away. You don't put them to bed to sleep it off. You don't wait an hour to see how they are. You don't worry about getting in trouble, because you will not be in trouble for keeping someone alive.

The thing I keep hearing is that people panic, tuck their mate into bed, and ring hours later. By then the brain's been without oxygen for too long. That's the gap between a scare and a funeral, and it's the only bit of this I really need you to take in.

Naloxone nasal spray reverses opioids. You can get it free from Brightpath, the drug and alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette. Anyone can ask, no names needed, and the training takes about ten minutes. They're open Monday to Friday, ten till four, and Thursdays until seven. If you've got a teenager in the house, it's worth knowing where that door is.

And please, talk to your kids this week. Not after half term, not when it comes up in the news again. This week. I had the chat with my lad last night over his tea. He's fourteen, he rolled his eyes at me, and then he asked me what pinpoint pupils actually meant. That's the whole reason you do it. He'd heard the phrase and had no idea what it looked like.

Last thing. The comments on the other thread, slagging off the kids and their parents — it helps nobody. Scared kids don't ring for help. That is the entire problem. If a young one thinks they'll be in more trouble than their mate is in danger, they'll wait, and waiting is what kills people.

Please share this, not just like it. Stick it on your own page, send it to the parents in your kid's year, put it in the family group chat. The ones who need it are exactly the ones who scroll past the official posts.

Thanks for reading. — Becky
